title: Find the message a ticket names

blocks.text: Your switch's support desk answers tickets from several acquirers. Each ticket gives a terminal ID, a STAN as the analyst typed it, and the moment the acquirer's records say the message was sent. The desk pastes the day's log into `TicketSearch.find`, which returns every logged message the ticket is about: the request and its answer, in log order, or nothing when the log never saw it.
`find` is written. Finish the three methods marked `TODO` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/TicketSearch.java`:

items: `stan(...)`: the ticket's STAN as a message carries it;
`sent(...)`: the ticket's moment as a message carries it;
`names(...)`: whether a logged message is one the ticket is about.

blocks.text: About six lines in total. The tests' logs hold terminals in more than one country, more than one day, and STANs that come round again; some tests run on a machine whose clock is not set to UTC.

cases.says: the request a ticket names and its answer are found, and no other message of the log
a ticket naming a message the log never saw finds nothing
another terminal's message with the same STAN and the same transmission time is not the one meant, so the terminal is part of the name
the same terminal reuses a STAN on another day, so the transmission time is part of the name
the ticket's time is compared with the transmission time in field 7, not with the terminal's local date and time in fields 12 and 13
field 7 is in UTC whatever time zone the machine running the search is set to
a STAN typed as 930 names the message whose field 11 is 000930

origin.section: 15.1. A Message Is Named by Its Terminal, STAN and Transmission Time, and the Time Is UTC

concepts: A logged message is found by its terminal, STAN and transmission time together, because STANs repeat across terminals and across days.
Field 7 holds the transmission time in UTC, while a log and fields 12 and 13 are local, so a ticket's time is matched against field 7.
